facts.fact_text: On 6 November 2005 parliamentary elections were held in Azerbaijan.
Following the announcement of the results of the parliamentary elections of 6 November 2005, the opposition electoral coalition Azadliq decided to hold demonstrations.
The demonstrations organised by Azadliq were intended to protest against alleged irregularities during the parliamentary elections of 6 November 2005.
On 26 November 2005 Azadliq held a demonstration at Galaba Square in Baku.
The demonstration on 26 November 2005 at Galaba Square was scheduled from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m.
The demonstration on 26 November 2005 at Galaba Square was held to protest against alleged election irregularities.
The applicant and her family participated in the demonstration on 26 November 2005 at Galaba Square in Baku.
Shortly after 5 p.m. on 26 November 2005, police began an operation to forcibly disperse the demonstrators at Galaba Square in Baku.
The police began the dispersal operation because the demonstration had continued beyond the authorised time-limit.
The dispersal operation on 26 November 2005 was conducted by riot police units.
The riot police units conducting the dispersal operation on 26 November 2005 were fully equipped with helmets, shields and truncheons.
According to the applicant, at around 4.45 p.m. on 26 November 2005 she was walking slowly to the edge of Galaba Square to wait for her husband to join her so that they could go home.
According to the applicant, she suddenly saw demonstrators beginning to run away from Galaba Square in a chaotic manner.
According to the applicant, at the same moment she saw demonstrators running away, she was hit on the head and back several times from behind.
According to the applicant, when she turned round after being hit, she was kicked in the chest and abdomen area.
According to the applicant, she managed to see that the persons who had kicked her were police officers in uniform equipped with a shield and truncheon.
According to the applicant, she lost consciousness and fell to the ground after being kicked by police officers.
Several news agencies managed to take photographs of the applicant lying unconscious on the ground surrounded by police officers.
Some of the photographs of the applicant lying unconscious on the ground were published in various newspapers and other news outlets.
The applicant lay in the same spot at Galaba Square for an unspecified period of time.
The applicant lost and regained consciousness several times while lying on the ground at Galaba Square.
According to the applicant, when she was conscious she saw several civilians trying to help her.
According to the applicant, the attempts by civilians to help her were actively prevented by the riot police and their police dogs.
According to the applicant, for a long time the riot police did not allow the ambulance units stationed at Galaba Square to provide her with any assistance.
According to the applicant, she was finally taken to hospital only after a number of civilians had urged the riot police to allow this.
The applicant was admitted to hospital at 6.30 p.m. on 26 November 2005.
The medical record concerning the applicant identifies her as Tahirova Surayya Musa gizi, born in 1953, living in Sumgayit, not working.
The medical record states that the applicant was admitted to hospital at 6.30–6.35 p.m. on 26 November 2005.
The medical record states that the applicant left the hospital on 27 November 2005.
The medical record records the applicant's full diagnosis as blunt trauma of the abdomen and diabetes.
The medical record states that the applicant was admitted to hospital with pain under the left ribs and general weakness.
According to the medical record, the applicant stated that she had been beaten up by police officers at Galaba Square on 26 November 2005 at around 5 p.m.
The medical record states that the applicant was taken to hospital from the scene of the incident by an ambulance.
The medical record states that on objective examination, on palpation the abdomen was not hard and was involved in respiration.
The medical record states that there was a little sharp pain under the applicant's left ribs on palpation.
The medical record states that ultrasound examination did not reveal free liquid or traumatic changes in the applicant's abdomen.
The medical record states that no fracture was apparent in the left part of the applicant's rib cage during X-ray examination.
The medical record states that the applicant was transferred for further examination and dynamic observation to the Reanimation and Intensive Therapy Department.
The medical record states that on 27 November 2005, at the request of the applicant and her relatives, she left the hospital in a stable condition.
The applicant spent the night of 26–27 November 2005 in hospital and received in-patient treatment.
The applicant's condition was stabilised and she was discharged from hospital the morning of 27 November 2005.

The Sabayil District Court held that the forcible dispersal of the demonstration on 26 November 2005 was lawful because the demonstrators had stayed at Galaba Square beyond 5 p.m., the time-limit permitted by the authorities.

The Sabayil District Court's judgment cited Article 7 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of the Republic of Azerbaijan, which provides the possibility to place restrictions on freedom of assembly for the prevention of disorder or crimes, for the protection of public interests and state security, and for the protection of other interests necessary in a democratic society.

The Sabayil District Court's judgment cited Article 14 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of the Republic of Azerbaijan, which entitles police authorities to warn organisers and participants that force will be used if an order to suspend the assembly and for its participants to disperse is not executed, and to use appropriate force to ensure the suspension of the assembly and the dispersal of its participants.
The Sabayil District Court found that the applicant had failed to submit any evidence proving that the police dispersed the gathering of 26 November 2005 before 5 p.m.

The Sabayil District Court found that police officers did not intervene in the demonstration until 5 p.m. and, only after the end of the determined period and following numerous warnings, the demonstrators were dispersed.

The Sabayil District Court found that the applicant had failed to submit reliable evidence proving that she was injured because she had been beaten by the police and as a result lost consciousness and fell to the ground.
On 11 August 2006 the Court of Appeal upheld the Sabayil District Court's judgment of 31 March 2006.

The Court of Appeal's judgment of 11 August 2006 is almost identical in its wording to the Sabayil District Court's judgment and reiterates the same reasons for the dismissal of the applicant's appeal.
On 12 December 2006 the Supreme Court of Azerbaijan upheld the judgments of the Sabayil District Court and the Court of Appeal.

Article 7 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides that any restriction on freedom of assembly may be placed only by law and for the purposes of protection of interests necessary in a democratic society, including: protection of the interests of public and state security; prevention of disturbance of public order; prevention of disorder or crime; protection of the health of the population; protection of morals; and protection of the rights and freedoms of others.

Article 14.I.3 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides that the police have the right to suspend an assembly, if the need arises, when the conduct of the assembly does not meet the conditions provided in the prior written notification.

Article 14.II of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides that the police have the right to inform organisers of and participants in an assembly of its suspension and dispersal, to order organisers and participants to use all available means for suspension of the assembly and dispersal of participants, to warn organisers and participants that force will be used if an order to suspend the assembly and for its participants to disperse is not executed, and to use appropriate force to ensure the suspension of the assembly and the dispersal of its participants.

Article 14.6 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides that use of physical force or special equipments by the police should in any case be proportional to the danger in question.

The representative of the Ministry of Internal Affairs submitted that the duration of the demonstration on 26 November 2005 had been determined in advance, scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. and end at 5 p.m.
The representative of the Ministry of Internal Affairs submitted that the demonstrators stayed at Galaba Square beyond 5 p.m. with the intention of continuing the demonstration unlawfully.

The representative of the Ministry of Internal Affairs submitted that soldiers of Internal Troops were not present at Galaba Square and that only police officers and the Riot Police Regiment were at the square.
The representative of the Ministry of Internal Affairs submitted that police officers asked demonstrators with loudspeakers to leave Galaba Square after the end of the demonstration.
The representative of the Ministry of Internal Affairs submitted that the police officers did not infringe the requirements of the legislation.
The representative of the Ministry of Internal Affairs was silent as to the applicant's particular complaint about her ill-treatment by the police.
On 31 March 2006 the Sabayil District Court dismissed the applicant's civil claim.
On 5 June 2006 the applicant appealed against the Sabayil District Court's judgment of 31 March 2006, reiterating her complaints.
Article 46(III) of the Constitution of the Republic of Azerbaijan provides that no one shall be subjected to torture or ill-treatment.
Article 46(III) of the Constitution of the Republic of Azerbaijan provides that no one shall be subjected to degrading treatment or punishment.
Article 49(I) of the Constitution of the Republic of Azerbaijan provides that everyone has the right to freely assemble together with others.

Article 49(II) of the Constitution of the Republic of Azerbaijan provides that everyone has the right, upon notification to relevant Government bodies in advance, to assemble peacefully with others, without arms, and to hold rallies, meetings, demonstrations, street marches and pickets.

Article 1 of the Law on Police of 28 October 1999 defines special equipments as truncheons, arm-restraining instruments, tear gas, rubber bullets, water cannons, special devices for forcible stopping of vehicles and other special equipments provided by the legislation of the Republic of Azerbaijan.
Article 26(VI) of the Law on Police of 28 October 1999 provides that use of physical force, special equipments or firearms in cases of extreme necessity shall be proportionate to the danger posed.

Article 26(VII) of the Law on Police of 28 October 1999 provides that the relevant police authorities must carry out an inquiry into every incident involving the use of physical force, special equipments or firearms by a police officer and must issue a pertinent opinion on its lawfulness.

Article 26(IX) of the Law on Police of 28 October 1999 provides that unlawful use of physical force, special equipments or firearms by a police officer entails the officer's responsibility under the relevant legislation.

Article 27(I)(1) of the Law on Police of 28 October 1999 provides that a police officer should use physical force, special equipments or firearms against a person only in the event of absolute necessity or necessary self-defence, after all other means of coercion have failed to produce the required result, and in proportion to the gravity of the offence and the personality of the offender.

Article 27(I)(5) of the Law on Police of 28 October 1999 provides that a police officer must provide the necessary medical aid to anyone injured as a result of the use of physical force, special equipments or firearms.

Article 27(I)(7) of the Law on Police of 28 October 1999 provides that a police officer must report in writing to the police office where he or she serves or to the police office of the area where firearms have been used, on the occasions he or she used physical force, special equipments or firearms.

Article 27(I)(8) of the Law on Police of 28 October 1999 provides that a police officer must inform the relevant prosecutor in writing of any use of physical force, special equipments or firearms within twenty-four hours.

Article 37.1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that, depending on the nature and severity of the offence, criminal prosecution shall be carried out in the form of private, public-private or public charges.

Article 37.2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that a private criminal prosecution shall take place only upon a complaint by the victim concerning offences under Articles 147 (defamation), 148 (insult), 165.1 (infringement of copyrights and related rights) and 166.1 (infringement of patent and invention rights) of the Criminal Code, and shall be discontinued in the event of reconciliation between the victim and the accused before the court deliberates.

Article 37.3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that a public-private criminal prosecution shall take place upon a complaint by the victim or, in the circumstances provided for in Article 37.5, on the initiative of the prosecutor for offences including Articles 127 (deliberate infliction of less serious injury to health), 128 (deliberate infliction of minor injury to health), 131.1 (infliction of less serious injury to health by negligence), 132–134 (beating; ill-treatment; death threat or threat of infliction of serious injury to health) and other specified articles of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

Article 37.5.2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that where no complaint is made by the victim, a public-private criminal prosecution may be initiated by the prosecutor if the offence was committed by or against a representative of the authority or other officials of State authorities.

Article 37.6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that in respect of offences not provided for in Articles 37.2 and 37.3, criminal prosecution shall be carried out in the form of public charges.

Article 39.1.8 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that a criminal prosecution may not be launched or, if already launched, shall be discontinued if the victim has not lodged a complaint in the case of a private prosecution or if the prosecutor does not take the initiative in launching the criminal prosecution in the case of public-private charges.

Article 46.1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that there shall be proper reason and grounds for the institution of criminal proceedings relating to a public or semi-public prosecution.

Article 46.2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that the reason for instituting criminal proceedings may be an application from an individual, information from a legal entity (official) or the media, or information directly obtained by the investigator or the prosecutor, concerning an offence committed or in preparation.

Article 3 of the Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials (adopted by the UN General Assembly Resolution 34/169 of 17 November 1979) provides that law enforcement officials may use force only when strictly necessary and to the extent required for the performance of their duty.

Article 5 of the Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials (adopted by the UN General Assembly Resolution 34/169 of 17 November 1979) provides that no law enforcement official may inflict, instigate or tolerate any act of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, nor may any law enforcement official invoke superior orders or exceptional circumstances as a justification of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

Principle 13 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (adopted by the Eighth UN Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, Cuba, 27 August to 7 September 1990) provides that in the dispersal of assemblies that are unlawful but non-violent, law enforcement officials shall avoid the use of force or, where that is not practicable, shall restrict such force to the minimum extent necessary.

Article 27(I)(8) of the Law on Police of 28 October 1999 provides that a police officer must inform the relevant prosecutor in writing of any use of physical force, special equipments or firearms within twenty-four hours.

Article 37.1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that, depending on the nature and severity of the offence, criminal prosecution shall be carried out in the form of private, public-private or public charges.

Article 37.2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that a private criminal prosecution shall take place only upon a complaint by the victim concerning offences under Articles 147 (defamation), 148 (insult), 165.1 (infringement of copyrights and related rights) and 166.1 (infringement of patent and invention rights) of the Criminal Code, and shall be discontinued in the event of reconciliation between the victim and the accused before the court deliberates.

Article 37.3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that a public-private criminal prosecution shall take place upon a complaint by the victim or, in the circumstances provided for in Article 37.5, on the initiative of the prosecutor for offences including Articles 127 (deliberate infliction of less serious injury to health), 128 (deliberate infliction of minor injury to health), 131.1 (infliction of less serious injury to health by negligence), 132–134 (beating; ill-treatment; death threat or threat of infliction of serious injury to health) and other specified articles of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

Article 37.5.2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that where no complaint is made by the victim, a public-private criminal prosecution may be initiated by the prosecutor if the offence was committed by or against a representative of the authority or other officials of State authorities.

Article 37.6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that in respect of offences not provided for in Articles 37.2 and 37.3, criminal prosecution shall be carried out in the form of public charges.

Article 39.1.8 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that a criminal prosecution may not be launched or, if already launched, shall be discontinued if the victim has not lodged a complaint in the case of a private prosecution or if the prosecutor does not take the initiative in launching the criminal prosecution in the case of public-private charges.

Article 46.1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that there shall be proper reason and grounds for the institution of criminal proceedings relating to a public or semi-public prosecution.

Article 46.2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Azerbaijan provides that the reason for instituting criminal proceedings may be an application from an individual, information from a legal entity (official) or the media, or information directly obtained by the investigator or the prosecutor, concerning an offence committed or in preparation.

Article 7 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides that any restriction on freedom of assembly may be placed only by law and for the purposes of protection of interests necessary in a democratic society, including: protection of the interests of public and state security; prevention of disturbance of public order; prevention of disorder or crime; protection of the health of the population; protection of morals; and protection of the rights and freedoms of others.

Article 14.I.3 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides that the police have the right to suspend an assembly, if the need arises, when the conduct of the assembly does not meet the conditions provided in the prior written notification.

Article 14.II of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides that the police have the right to inform organisers of and participants in an assembly of its suspension and dispersal, to order organisers and participants to use all available means for suspension of the assembly and dispersal of participants, to warn organisers and participants that force will be used if an order to suspend the assembly and for its participants to disperse is not executed, and to use appropriate force to ensure the suspension of the assembly and the dispersal of its participants.

Article 14.6 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides that use of physical force or special equipments by the police should in any case be proportional to the danger in question.

Article 3 of the Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials (adopted by the UN General Assembly Resolution 34/169 of 17 November 1979) provides that law enforcement officials may use force only when strictly necessary and to the extent required for the performance of their duty.

Article 5 of the Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials (adopted by the UN General Assembly Resolution 34/169 of 17 November 1979) provides that no law enforcement official may inflict, instigate or tolerate any act of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, nor may any law enforcement official invoke superior orders or exceptional circumstances as a justification of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

Principle 13 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (adopted by the Eighth UN Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, Cuba, 27 August to 7 September 1990) provides that in the dispersal of assemblies that are unlawful but non-violent, law enforcement officials shall avoid the use of force or, where that is not practicable, shall restrict such force to the minimum extent necessary.

The OSCE/ODIHR Election Observation Mission Final Report on the parliamentary elections of 6 November 2005 (dated 1 February 2006) states that Azadliq and other opposition parties organised another protest meeting on 26 November 2005 at Galaba Square.

The OSCE/ODIHR Election Observation Mission Final Report on the parliamentary elections of 6 November 2005 (dated 1 February 2006) states that police dispersed the participants of the 26 November 2005 meeting at Galaba Square using considerable force, immediately after expiration of the allotted time for the meeting.
